title: Sparse Probe Overfitting: Deception Detection Probes Trained on Narrow Scenarios Fail on Novel Schemes

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tests the generalization of deception probes, which is central to their practical value. If probes only detect training-distribution deception types, they are weak against capable schemers. Clear safety implication.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Training probes on one deception type and evaluating on others is a standard ML generalization experiment. Dataset construction for different deception types (lies, omissions, misleading implications) is the main challenge but is feasible with careful prompt engineering.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable: probe accuracy degradation table across deception types. Could be tightened to 3 deception types with a single model. The dataset construction for novel deception types adds some scope uncertainty.

novelty.reasoning: Deception probe generalization is actively studied but not fully resolved. (1) 'Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes' (OpenReview) demonstrates linear probes achieving AUROC >0.96 for deception detection including sandbagging and insider trading scenarios. (2) 'Benchmarking Deception Probes via Black-to-White Performance Boosts' (arXiv:2507.12691, 2025) tests probes against black-box baselines and distributional shift. (3) 'Difficulties with Evaluating a Deception Detector for AIs' (arXiv:2511.22662, 2025) raises fundamental concerns about testing generalization without examples of genuine strategic deception. Existing work partially addresses the generalization question but focuses on within-framework transfers. The specific framing of training on one deception type (lies) and testing on categorically different types (omissions, misleading implications) with a systematic taxonomy adds value, though the general concern is well-established.
